core: Working definition of pharmacodynamics: what a drug does to the body, and the relationship between drug concentration at its sites of action and the effects that follow
The receptor idea: drugs produce effects by attaching to specific protein targets, pictured as a lock and key
Response types: agonist, antagonist, partial agonist, each with an original example
Dose and response: more drug, more effect up to the drug's maximum (ceiling) effect, with the honest caveat that response is not a perfect straight line
Therapeutic window: the dose range that works without harm; narrow windows need monitoring
Individual variation: age, body size, genetics, and other drugs change response — the same drug is not the same for everyone
supporting: Minimum effective concentration as the threshold below which no therapeutic effect appears
Pharmacogenomics as the genetics of drug response
Selectivity: a drug that fits few receptor types tends to cause fewer unintended effects
outOfScope: Pharmacology foundations (drug classes, nomenclature, sources, rights) — own sibling topic
Pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) — own sibling topic
Medication safety (rights of administration, error prevention, documentation) — own sibling topic
Molecular-level receptor biology and biochemistry — owned by the biology subject
Dosing advice or drug-specific doses — never taught in this lesson

claims.claim: Pharmacodynamics is the study of what a drug does to the body — the effects a drug produces at its sites of action, involving receptor binding, postreceptor effects, and chemical interactions.

Most drug targets are receptors — protein molecules on the surface of or inside cells — that naturally bind the body's own signaling chemicals such as hormones and neurotransmitters; a drug that resembles a natural messenger can occupy the same receptor, and that interaction produces the drug's effect.

An agonist binds a receptor and activates it, mimicking the body's own response; an antagonist binds without activating and blocks the natural signal; a partial agonist activates the receptor but less strongly than a full agonist.

A drug must reach a minimum effective concentration at its site of action before a therapeutic effect appears, and response generally grows with dose up to the drug's maximum attainable response (ceiling effect), beyond which more drug adds no benefit.

The therapeutic window (therapeutic index) is the dose range that is both safe and effective; a narrow window means small dose changes risk toxicity or loss of effect, which is why some drugs require blood-level monitoring.

Individual variation in drug response comes from age (the very young and very old are the most sensitive), body size (larger bodies may need larger doses; pediatric dosing is often per kilogram), genetics, and other drugs a person takes.

Pharmacogenomics is the study of how genes affect a person's response to drugs; many drugs are 'one size fits all' even though people are not, which is why some people benefit, some do not respond, and some have adverse reactions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'side effects' and 'adverse drug reactions' are the same thing.
positions: Some sources use the terms interchangeably (noted by OpenStax Pharmacology for Nurses).
Others differentiate: side effects are secondary, usually mild and predictable effects; adverse drug reactions are harmful effects seen at therapeutic doses (OpenStax's working distinction).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not teach this distinction (medication-safety sibling territory) and only uses the concept-level phrase 'harm' when describing toxicity risk past the ceiling, which all sources support.

conflictingEvidence.issue: 'Therapeutic index' versus 'therapeutic window' terminology and framing.
positions: Merck Manual Professional defines therapeutic index as the ratio of the minimum toxic concentration to the median effective concentration.
OpenStax Pharmacology for Nurses describes the therapeutic index as the range of dosing that is both safe and effective, and uses 'therapeutic window' for the same idea.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both agree on the practical meaning — a dose range that works without harm, narrower being riskier. The lesson states the simple, shared meaning and notes the two names refer to the same idea.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's generic boilerplate (e.g., 'Pharmacodynamics is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations', 'a label on a toolbox drawer', 'Think of pharmacodynamics as a label on a toolbox drawer') — discarded as machine-generated filler with no source support.
The draft's definition of pharmacodynamics as merely 'a concept students use to organize information' — replaced with the attributed working definition (what the drug does to the body).
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the draft's toolbox-drawer framing with the sourced working definition from OpenStax and Merck Manual Professional.

Added the receptor/lock-and-key concept, agonist/antagonist/partial-agonist response types, dose-response ceiling, therapeutic window, and the four individual-variation factors (age, size, genetics, other drugs), none of which the draft covered.
Replaced all five draft questions with scenario-based items whose keys are verified against the evidence and spread across A/B/C/D.
Removed all dosing language: the lesson teaches concepts only, per the subject's clinical-safety caution.

sourceRecords.title: Pharmacology for Nurses (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-22 via Wayback captures of sections 1.4 'Special Considerations' (capture 20260417002753) and 2.2 'Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics' (capture 20260414122653) at the canonical openstax.org URLs. Section 2.2 supplies the working definition ('what the drug does to the body'), the receptor and lock-and-key description, agonist/antagonist/partial-agonist definitions, the minimum effective concentration, the therapeutic index as the safe-and-effective dose range, and genetic/age/other-drug variability. Section 1.4 supplies the body-size factor (per-kilogram pediatric dosing; larger bodies may need larger doses) and that the very young and very old are most sensitive to drugs. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Overview of Pharmacodynamics (Merck Manual Professional Edition)
sourceRecords.provider: Merck & Co., Inc. (Merck Manual Professional Edition)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Full review June 2025, peer-reviewed. Supplies the formal definition (biochemical, physiologic, and molecular effects of drugs on the body; receptor binding, postreceptor effects, chemical interactions), the dose-and-response framing, that response depends on drug binding to its target with concentration at the receptor influencing effect, and that pharmacodynamics is affected by disorder, increasing age, other drugs, and genetic mutations. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Dose-Response Relationships (Merck Manual Professional Edition)
sourceRecords.provider: Merck & Co., Inc. (Merck Manual Professional Edition)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Full review June 2025, peer-reviewed. Supplies the ceiling effect (maximal efficacy, greatest attainable response), the statement that response to concentration is often nonlinear, biologic variation among people given the same dose, and the therapeutic index (ratio of minimum toxic concentration to median effective concentration) with the note that increasing the dose of a small-index drug raises the probability of toxicity. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is pharmacogenomics? (MedlinePlus Genetics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (NLM/.gov). Supplies the genetics claim: pharmacogenomics is the study of how genes affect a person's response to drugs; many drugs are 'one size fits all' but do not work the same way for everyone; it is hard to predict who will benefit, who will not respond, and who will experience adverse reactions. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
